verdict.rationale: One body of vocabulary places the Son before creation and inside the divine being. John 1:1 uses the ongoing past form of the verb 'to be' (eimi, morph V-IAI-3S, the imperfect, an ongoing or repeated past action) three times for 'the Word' (ho logos) at 'the beginning' (arche), contrasted with the completed past form (aorist, a completed past action) of 'to come to be' (ginomai) for created things. John 17:5 and 17:24 set shared glory and the Father's love for 'me' 'before the world existed' (pro tou ton kosmon einai) and 'before the foundation of the world' (pro katabolēs kosmou). Colossians 1:15-17 makes the Son the sphere, agent, and goal of all creation and 'before all things' (pro pantōn). Hebrews 1:6 calls him 'the firstborn' (ton prōtotokon) already when God brings him into the world. The sending verbs act on a Son already 'one-of-a-kind' (monogenēs), with 'I have sent' (apostellō) in the perfect (a completed action whose result still stands) in 1 John 4:9, and 'he gave' (didōmi) in the aorist (a completed past action) in John 3:16. But a second body of vocabulary, the begetting verbs 'to bear, beget' (yalad) in Psalm 2:7 (in the qal, the simple active form of the Hebrew verb, perfect form) and 'to beget' (gennaō) in Hebrews 1:5, Hebrews 5:5, and Acts 13:33 (perfect 'I have begotten' (gegennēka) with 'today' (sēmeron)), is attached by the canon to a moment in time, the resurrection and enthronement, and Hebrews 1:5b quotes the Davidic adoption formula of 2 Samuel 7:14. The begetting words alone do not rank these two patterns, so the affirm rests on the durative (ongoing) and pre-creation terms, not on the begetting terms.

scripture.force: 'In the beginning was the Word' (ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος), with 'was' (ἦν) tagged V-IAI-3S (imperfect of 'to be' (εἰμί), an ongoing or repeated past action) three times, placing 'the Word' (Logos) in ongoing, continuous being at the absolute origin, with the 'toward God' (πρὸς τὸν θεόν) relation. Verse 3 shifts to the completed past form (aorist, a completed past action) 'came to be' (ἐγένετο) for created things, so 'the Word' (Logos) stands on the uncreated side of the 'was' versus 'came-to-be' contrast.

'This one was in the beginning toward God' (οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεόν) repeats the ongoing past form 'was' (ἦν, imperfect of 'to be', an ongoing or repeated past action) and the 'toward' (πρός) relation, locking the Father and 'Word' (Logos) distinction into the pre-creation frame before any begetting language appears.

'glory as of the only one (one-of-a-kind) from a father' (δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρός) pairs 'one-of-a-kind' (μονογενής, monogenes) with 'from a father' (παρὰ πατρός). The same word 'one-of-a-kind' (μονογενής, monogenes) is used in the canon of ordinary only-children (Luke 7:12, Luke 8:42, Hebrews 11:17 of Isaac), so it lexically means 'only, unique-kind', not 'created' or 'originated'.

'the only-one (one-of-a-kind) God' (μονογενὴς θεός, in the earliest witnesses) or 'the only-one (one-of-a-kind) Son' (ὁ μονογενὴς υἱός, in the Byzantine tradition), 'the one being in the bosom of the Father' (ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός). The present participle 'the one being' (ὁ ὤν) marks ongoing relational location, not an event of becoming Son. Both variant readings apply 'one-of-a-kind' (μονογενής, monogenes) to the Son.

'glorify me, Father, alongside yourself with the glory which I was having alongside you before the world existed' (δόξασόν με σύ, πάτερ, παρὰ σεαυτῷ τῇ δόξῃ ᾗ εἶχον πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι παρὰ σοί). The ongoing past form 'I was having' (εἶχον, imperfect, an ongoing or repeated past action) with 'before' (πρό) plus the 'of-which' (genitive, the 'from-X or of-X' grammatical form) places shared glory and the 'alongside you' (παρὰ σοί) relation prior to the existence of 'the world' (κόσμος, kosmos).

'you loved me before the foundation of the world' (ἠγάπησάς με πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου), with the completed past form 'you loved' (ἠγάπησάς, aorist, a completed past action) and 'before the foundation of the world' (πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου) locating the Father's love directed at 'me' before the foundation of the world. The object of that love is the personal 'me' of the speaker, prior to creation.

'image of the invisible God, firstborn of all creation' (εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου, πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως). 'Firstborn' (πρωτότοκος, prototokos, 9 occurrences) carries both birth-order 'firstborn' (Luke 2:7) and rank or preeminence (read against verse 16 'because in him all things were created' (ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα)). The grounding 'because' (ὅτι) makes him agent of all creation, so the 'of-which' form (genitive, the 'from-X or of-X' grammatical form) is of rank, not of membership in 'creation' (κτίσις, ktisis).

'because in him all things were created' (ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα), then the perfect (a completed action whose result still stands) 'all things through him and toward him have been created' (τὰ πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν ἔκτισται). The triad 'in' (ἐν), 'through' (διά), 'toward' (εἰς) makes the Son the sphere, agent, and goal of all creation. If 'all things' (τὰ πάντα) is created in and through him, he is not a member of 'all things' (τὰ πάντα).

'and he himself is before all things, and in him all things hold together' (καὶ αὐτός ἐστιν πρὸ πάντων, καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκεν). The emphatic 'he himself' (αὐτός) with the present-tense 'is' (ἐστιν, ongoing, simple statement of fact) plus 'before' (πρό) marks personal priority over 'all things' (τὰ πάντα), and the perfect 'have held together' (συνέστηκεν, a completed action whose result still stands) marks his ongoing sustaining function.

'and when again he brings the firstborn into the inhabited world' (ὅταν δὲ πάλιν εἰσαγάγῃ τὸν πρωτότοκον εἰς τὴν οἰκουμένην). The Son is already named 'the firstborn' (τὸν πρωτότοκον) at the point God brings him into 'the inhabited world' (τὴν οἰκουμένην), so the firstborn status precedes his entry into the world rather than being conferred by it.

'but to the Son: your throne, O God, is for the age of the age' (πρὸς δὲ τὸν υἱόν: ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ θεός, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος). The Father addresses the Son with 'O God' (ὁ θεός, in the direct-address form (vocative, the 'O X' form of address)) and an everlasting throne, citing Psalm 45:6 (store cross-ref Hebrews 1:8 to Psalm 45:6) as direct divine address to the Son.

'radiance of the glory and exact impress of his being' (ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ). 'Radiance' (ἀπαύγασμα, apaugasma) and 'exact impress' (χαρακτήρ, charakter) describe origin-from but not temporal beginning. Radiance is co-temporal with its source, so the lexis describes derivation without a point of coming-to-be.

'God has sent his only-one (one-of-a-kind) Son into the world' (τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ τὸν μονογενῆ ἀπέσταλκεν ὁ θεὸς εἰς τὸν κόσμον). 'He has sent' (ἀπέσταλκεν) is tagged V-RAI-3S (perfect, a completed action whose result still stands), and the Son is already qualified 'only-one (one-of-a-kind)' (μονογενῆ, monogenes) when sent. The sending acts on an existing unique Son, it does not make him Son.

'he gave his only-one (one-of-a-kind) Son' (τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ τὸν μονογενῆ ἔδωκεν). 'He gave' (ἔδωκεν) is tagged V-AAI-3S (aorist, a completed past action), acting on a Son already designated 'only-one (one-of-a-kind)' (μονογενῆ, monogenes). The giving does not constitute the sonship.

The Hebrew frames the line as a 'decree' (חֹק, choq) the LORD spoke: 'you are my son, today I have begotten you' (בְּנִי אַתָּה, הַיּוֹם יְלִדְתִּיךָ). 'I have begotten you' (יְלִדְתִּיךָ) is the verb 'to bear, beget' (yalad) tagged HVqp1cs (qal, the simple active form of the Hebrew verb, perfect form, first-person singular with second-masculine-singular suffix). 'To bear, beget' (yalad) occurs 466 times and dominantly means literal physical begetting (Genesis genealogies), so its native sense is point-of-origin, but here it is the content of a decree spoken 'today' (הַיּוֹם), a coronation idiom. The word carries origin sense but its frame is enthronement declaration.

'you are my son, today I have begotten you' (υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε), with 'I have begotten' (γεγέννηκά, from 'to beget' (gennaō)) tagged V-RAI-1S (perfect, a completed action whose result still stands) plus the adverb 'today' (σήμερον, semeron). The verse then quotes 2 Samuel 7:14 (store cross-ref Hebrews 1:5 to 2 Samuel 7:14) in the future tense, 'I will be to him for a father and he himself will be to me for a son' (ἔσομαι αὐτῷ εἰς πατέρα καὶ αὐτὸς ἔσται μοι εἰς υἱόν), the Davidic covenant formula. The begetting plus 'today' plus future adoption formula is a royal-installation matrix.

'having raised up Jesus ... you are my son, today I have begotten you' (ἀναστήσας Ἰησοῦν ... υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε). The completed past participle (aorist participle) 'having raised up' (ἀναστήσας) ties the 'today' (σήμερον, semeron) of the begetting decree explicitly to the resurrection day, so the canon itself applies the begetting language of Psalm 2:7 to a moment in time.

'therefore also the holy one being born will be called Son of God' (διὸ καὶ τὸ γεννώμενον ἅγιον κληθήσεται υἱὸς θεοῦ). The future passive 'will be called' (κληθήσεται) and the present participle 'the one being born' (τὸ γεννώμενον, from 'to beget' (gennaō)) attach the title 'Son of God' to the one conceived and born, so the sonship title is here predicated of the incarnate child. The verb is 'is called', which does not by itself decide whether the title names a pre-existing relation or originates at birth.

'the LORD acquired/possessed me as the beginning of his way' (יהוה קָנָנִי רֵאשִׁית דַּרְכּוֹ). The verb 'to possess, acquire' (qanah) carries 'possess' or 'acquire' as well as 'create'. The Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, LXX) renders this as 'he created me' (ἔκτισέν με), which was used against eternal sonship, but the subject is personified Wisdom in poetry, and identifying that figure with the Son is a typological judgment, not a direct lemma identification of the Son.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'today I have begotten you' (הַיּוֹם יְלִדְתִּיךָ) uses 'to bear, beget' (yalad) in the qal (the simple active form of the Hebrew verb), perfect form, whose dominant canon sense across 466 occurrences is literal physical begetting, a point of origin. Here it is the content of a 'decree' (חֹק, choq) spoken 'today' (הַיּוֹם), the royal-coronation idiom of the Davidic Psalms. The begetting word supplies an origin sense, but the 'today' frame redirects it to an enthronement declaration of an already addressed son, so the verse neither establishes nor excludes eternal sonship on lexis alone.

'today I have begotten you' (σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε, with the perfect form 'I have begotten' from 'to beget' (gennaō), a completed action whose result still stands, plus 'today' (semeron)) is paired in the same verse with the future Davidic adoption formula of 2 Samuel 7:14, 'I will be to him for a father, he will be to me for a son' (ἔσομαι ... εἰς πατέρα, ἔσται ... εἰς υἱόν). Acts 13:33 fixes the 'today' (σήμερον, semeron) to the resurrection. So the canon applies the begetting and son-installation language to a moment in time, which is why the begetting texts cannot by themselves carry the eternal verdict. The affirm rests on the separate durative (ongoing) and pre-creation vocabulary, not on these verses.

'having raised up Jesus' (ἀναστήσας Ἰησοῦν) fixes the 'today' (σήμερον, semeron) of Psalm 2:7 to the resurrection day. This corroborates that the begetting decree is applied as public declaration at an event, not as a statement about the Son coming into existence. It complicates but does not overturn, since the Johannine and Pauline pre-creation terms describe a relation already in place.

'will be called Son of God' (κληθήσεται υἱὸς θεοῦ, future passive) attaches the title 'Son of God' to 'the one being born' (τὸ γεννώμενον, from 'to beget' (gennaō)), the one being conceived and born. The verb 'is called' does not lexically decide whether the title names a pre-existing relation now revealed in the incarnation or originates at conception. The word underdetermines the question, so this remains unresolved at the lexical level and is the clearest single-verse pressure point against an eternal reading.

'firstborn of all creation' (πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως, from 'firstborn' (prototokos) and 'creation' (ktisis)) in isolation can read as first member of 'creation' (κτίσις, ktisis). The causal 'because' (ὅτι) in verse 16 makes him the agent in whom and through whom 'all things' (τὰ πάντα) was created, which rules out membership in 'all things' (τὰ πάντα). 'Firstborn' (πρωτότοκος, prototokos, 9 occurrences) bears both birth-order and rank senses, and Hebrews 1:6 shows the Son is already 'firstborn' (πρωτότοκος, prototokos) before being brought into the world, so 'rank' or 'preeminence' is the contextually forced sense here.

Hebrew 'he acquired/possessed me' (קָנָנִי, from 'to possess, acquire' (qanah)) is ambiguous between 'acquire' and 'create', and the Greek Old Testament's (Septuagint, LXX) 'he created me' (ἔκτισέν με) was used in the fourth-century dispute. Lexically the identification of personified Wisdom with the pre-incarnate Son is a typological judgment, not a direct lemma identification, so this verse does not by itself overturn the Johannine and Pauline pattern.

'the Father is greater than I' (ὁ πατὴρ μείζων μού ἐστιν) has been read against co-equal sonship. 'Greater' (μείζων, meizon) in this discourse follows the sending and return frame ('I am going to the Father' (ὑπάγω πρὸς τὸν πατέρα)), addressing ordering during the incarnation, not a temporal-beginning vocabulary for the Son.

variant_units_examined.note: The earliest witnesses (P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) read 'only-one (one-of-a-kind) God' (μονογενὴς θεός, with 'one-of-a-kind' (monogenes)), the Byzantine tradition reads 'the only-one (one-of-a-kind) Son' (ὁ μονογενὴς υἱός). Both apply 'one-of-a-kind' (μονογενής, monogenes) to the Son 'in the bosom of the Father' with the present participle 'the one being' (ὁ ὤν), so the verdict holds across both readings.

The variant at the end of the verse reads 'scepter of his kingdom' (ῥάβδος τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ) versus 'scepter of your kingdom' (with σου, your). Either reading preserves the address 'your throne, O God' (ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ θεός) to the Son, so the everlasting kingdom predication is undisturbed.

Minor word-order variants do not affect 'he gave the only-one (one-of-a-kind) Son' (τὸν υἱὸν τὸν μονογενῆ ἔδωκεν, with 'one-of-a-kind' (monogene)). The unique-Son predicate and the completed past form 'he gave' (aorist of giving, a completed past action) are stable.

variants.note: The critical edition of New Testament textual variants (ECM apparatus) is not yet published for John, Colossians, Psalms, or Hebrews (none of the anchors fall in the ingested 3 John window). Variant assessments are drawn from the NA28 apparatus and INTF NTVMR images, not from CBGM data.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the ongoing past form 'was' (ἦν, imperfect of 'to be', an ongoing or repeated past action), the 'before' (πρό) and 'alongside' (παρά) prepositions with creation-frame 'of-which' forms (genitives, the 'from-X or of-X' grammatical form) in John 17:5, 17:24, and Colossians 1:17, the 'firstborn' (πρωτότοκος, prototokos) that precedes the Son's entry into the world in Hebrews 1:6, and the sending of an already 'one-of-a-kind' (monogenes) Son (1 John 4:9 perfect, John 3:16 aorist) as marking a pre-temporal Father-Son relation. The begetting texts are read as enthronement declarations of an already existing Son.

Takes the begetting vocabulary at its strongest. 'To bear, beget' (yalad) in Psalm 2:7, qal (the simple active form of the Hebrew verb) perfect, and 'to beget' (gennaō) in Hebrews 1:5, Hebrews 5:5, and Acts 13:33, perfect (a completed action whose result still stands) with 'today' (σήμερον, semeron), are tied by the canon itself to a moment, and Acts 13:33 anchors the 'today' to the resurrection. On this reading the Son title or its full investiture is constituted or publicly declared at an event in time. This lens grants the pre-existence of 'the Word' (Logos) but locates the formal sonship at enthronement, and the begetting words do not lexically rank against it.

Leans on Luke 1:35, where 'will be called Son of God' (κληθήσεται υἱὸς θεοῦ) attaches the title to 'the one being born' (τὸ γεννώμενον, from 'to beget' (gennaō)), the one conceived and born. On this reading sonship names the relation the eternal Word enters at the incarnation. It must still account for John 17:24, the Father loving 'me' before the foundation of the world, which addresses the same personal subject prior to creation.

Accepts pre-existence but reads 'greater' (μείζων, meizon) in John 14:28 and Father-as-source language as marking ontological ranking. Lexically this still yields an asymmetrical relation rather than a temporal beginning for the Son.

Treats Psalm 2:7 plus the resurrection 'today' (σήμερον, semeron) of Acts 13:33 as constituting sonship at the resurrection. This cannot account for the ongoing past form 'was' (ἦν, imperfect of 'to be', an ongoing or repeated past action) of John 1:1-2, the 'before the world existed' (πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι) of John 17:5, or the pre-creation 'image' (εἰκών, eikon) and agency predications of Colossians 1:15-17, which describe a relation already in place before creation.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on two bodies of vocabulary that do not rank against each other. One body (the ongoing past form 'was' (ἦν, imperfect of 'to be', an ongoing or repeated past action), 'before' (πρό) and 'alongside' (παρά) with creation-frame 'of-which' forms (genitives, the 'from-X or of-X' grammatical form), the 'in' (ἐν), 'through' (διά), 'toward' (εἰς) agency triad, 'firstborn' (πρωτότοκος, prototokos) preceding entry into the world, the sending of an already 'one-of-a-kind' (monogenes) Son) describes a pre-creation Father-Son relation. The other body (the begetting verbs 'to bear, beget' (yalad) and 'to beget' (gennaō), attached by the canon to 'today' (σήμερον, semeron) and the resurrection, with the future Davidic adoption formula of 2 Samuel 7:14) attaches son-installation language to a moment in time. The affirm rests on the first body, the begetting texts are read as declaration rather than origination, and a reader who weights the begetting texts as constitutive reaches a different verdict.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Examine whether the Son is presented in the canon as having a temporal origin or an event that constitutes his sonship, or as eternally and relationally Son of the Father.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem assumes the conciliar (council-derived) vocabulary 'co-eternal' and 'co-equal', which is post-canonical formulation. The verdict is derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form lets the lexical pattern speak first. The verdict affirms unchanged from the prior file. The lexical evidence still supports affirm via the durative (ongoing) and pre-creation vocabulary, but confidence is lowered from high to medium because the begetting verbs 'to bear, beget' (yalad) and 'to beget' (gennaō) carry an origin sense and the canon attaches 'today, I have begotten you' to the resurrection and enthronement (Acts 13:33), and Luke 1:35 ties the 'called Son of God' title to the one being born. So the begetting and title vocabulary underdetermines whether sonship is eternal or constituted at an event. This file is flagged 'lexically-disputed' for that reason.

lay_summary: Two sets of words pull in different directions, which is why this question is genuinely contested at the text level. One set clearly puts the Son before the created order. John 1:1 uses the durative 'was', the ongoing past form of the verb 'to be' (eimi), three times for 'the Word' (logos) at the beginning, while verse 3 switches to 'came to be' for created things, so the Word sits on the uncreated side. John 17:5 and 17:24 have Jesus speak of glory he had and of the Father loving 'me' before the world existed and before its foundation. Colossians 1:15-17 makes the Son the one in whom, through whom, and for whom everything was made, and before all things. Hebrews 1:6 already calls him 'the firstborn' (prototokos) when God brings him into the world. The word 'only-begotten' or 'one-of-a-kind' (monogenes) is used elsewhere of ordinary only-children, so it means unique, not created, and the verbs of sending and giving (1 John 4:9, John 3:16) act on a Son who is already unique. The other set of words attaches sonship to a moment. Psalm 2:7 says 'today I have begotten you', using the begetting verb 'to bear, beget' (yalad), whose ordinary sense across hundreds of uses is literal physical birth, and it sits inside a royal decree. Hebrews 1:5, Hebrews 5:5, and Acts 13:33 quote this with 'today' (semeron) and a perfect 'have begotten' (gegenneka, from gennao), and Acts ties the today to the resurrection, while Hebrews 1:5 also quotes the royal adoption promise 'I will be his father, he shall be my son'. Luke 1:35 says the child to be born will be called Son of God. The begetting and title words by themselves do not say whether sonship is eternal or begun at an event. The verdict lands on affirm because the durative and before-creation words describe a relation already in place, and the begetting texts read naturally as a declaration or enthronement of an already existing Son. But because the begetting vocabulary genuinely carries an origin sense and the canon applies it to a point in time, the confidence is medium and readers who weight those texts as constitutive reach a different conclusion.
